name: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
description: Legendary ascending multi-tiered botanical palace terraces, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
history: Reputedly built by King Nebuchadnezzar II for his Median wife Queen Amytis, who longed for the lush, forested mountains of her homeland. The gardens featured ascending series of tiered stone terraces with tropical flora and gravity-fed irrigation.
construction: Engineered with waterproofed vaulted stone foundations covered in bitumen, reeds, and baked brick, using innovative Archimedes screw-style water wheels lifting water from the Euphrates river.
architecture: Tiered ziggurat-like terraced structure rising over 23 meters into the air, creating the illusion of a floating mountain garden in the Mesopotamian desert.
significance: One of the canonical Seven Wonders of the Ancient World chronicled by Strabo, Diodorus Siculus, and Antipater of Sidon.
currentStatus: Destroyed after the 1st century CE due to earthquakes and warfare; archaeological excavations near Al-Hillah, Iraq continue to seek definitive structural foundations.
wonderStatus: Destroyed (after 1st century CE by earthquakes & erosion)
wonderReplacedYear: July 7, 2007 (Succeeded by New 7 Wonders Modern Registry)
wonderReplacedBy: Replaced in the modern global canon by the New 7 Wonders campaign
wonderHistoricalContext: Celebrated in ancient Hellenistic literature for its unprecedented hydraulic irrigation and botanical grandeur. The gardens gradually fell into ruin after the fall of Babylon and were toppled by seismic tremors and Euphrates floods by the 1st century CE.
